section.title: Benediction and Farewell
section.sectionRationale: The letter closes with one of the great benedictions of Scripture and a few personal words. The blessing gathers the whole message: the God of peace raised the great Shepherd from the dead by the blood of the eternal covenant, and He now equips His people to do His will. The farewell mentions Timothy, sends greetings, and ends with grace.
section.thesis: The God of peace, who by the blood of the eternal covenant raised the Lord Jesus, the great Shepherd of the sheep, is able to equip His people with everything good to do His will and to work in them what pleases Him through Jesus Christ, to whom belongs eternal glory; and so the letter ends with a plea to heed its exhortation, personal news, greetings, and grace.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the closing benediction, invoking the God of peace who raised the great Shepherd by the blood of the eternal covenant to equip His people; and the farewell, with a final appeal, news of Timothy, greetings, and a parting word of grace.

units.label: The benediction
units.note: the God of peace and the great Shepherd

verses.text: Now may the God of {{eirene|peace}}, who through the blood of the eternal {{diatheke|covenant}} brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great {{poimen|Shepherd}} of the sheep,
{{katartizo|equip}} you with every good thing to do His will. And may He accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

units.label: Final words and greetings
units.note: grace be with all of you

verses.text: I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly.
Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you.
Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy send you greetings.
Grace be with all of you.

eirene.gloss: Peace, wholeness, reconciliation. God is the God of peace, the one who has made peace between Himself and His people through the blood of the covenant, and who now settles and completes His people in that peace.

diatheke.gloss: A covenant. The eternal covenant is the new covenant sealed by Christ's blood, everlasting and unbreakable; it is by this blood that God raised the Shepherd and secures His flock forever.

poimen.gloss: A shepherd. Jesus is the great Shepherd of the sheep, raised from the dead to lead, feed, and keep His flock; the title gathers the Old Testament hope of the shepherd who tends God's people.

katartizo.gloss: To equip, mend, complete, put fully in order, as a net is mended or a bone set. God equips His people with everything good to do His will, working in them what is pleasing in His sight.

basic.context: Hebrews ends with a magnificent blessing and a warm farewell. The benediction sums up the whole letter in one sentence: the God of peace raised Jesus, the great Shepherd, from the dead by the blood of the eternal covenant, and this God equips His people to do His will. Then the writer asks them to receive his exhortation, shares news of Timothy, passes on greetings, and closes with grace.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the benediction as a summary of Hebrews: covenant, blood, resurrection, priest-shepherd, and God working in us. It is also a prayer, asking God to do what the letter has urged. The farewell gives rare personal detail in an otherwise anonymous letter.
basic.originalLanguages: The God of eirēnē, peace, raised Jesus by the blood of the eternal diathēkē, covenant. Jesus is the great poimēn, Shepherd. God will katartizō, equip, His people to do His will.
basic.typology: The great Shepherd fulfills the Old Testament promise of God shepherding His flock and of a coming shepherd-king. The eternal covenant fulfills the new covenant promised through Jeremiah and sealed in Christ's blood.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Lord raised from the dead, the great Shepherd of the sheep, and the mediator through whom God works what pleases Him. The resurrection, mentioned explicitly here, crowns the letter's portrait of His finished work.
basic.god: God is the God of peace who raised Jesus and who equips His people. He works in us what is pleasing to Him, so that even our obedience is His gift, all to His eternal glory.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 63 speaks of the shepherd brought up from the sea. John 10 calls Jesus the good shepherd. Philippians 2 says God works in us to will and to act.
basic.oneStory: The letter closes by gathering its whole message into a blessing: the God of peace has raised the great Shepherd by covenant blood and now equips His people, leading His flock to glory.

context.literary:
The closing of Hebrews is one long Greek sentence in verses 20 and 21, a prayer that is also a summary. It has a skeleton the reader can see: the God of peace, described by what He did, "brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus", described again as "that great Shepherd of the sheep", and further by the means, "the blood of the eternal covenant", is asked to equip you and to accomplish in us what pleases Him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory. The sentence then closes with a doxology and an Amen, so that the whole letter is brought to rest in praise.

Almost every major theme of the letter is gathered in this one sentence. Peace recalls the covenant of peace promised through the prophets. The blood and the covenant recall chapters 8 to 10. The word Lord and the name Jesus, together with the phrase Jesus Christ, bring the person to the front. The Shepherd comes from the Old Testament picture of God and His king. The equipping looks to the readers' obedience, and the whole is for glory.

Verse 22 shifts abruptly, from a prayer to a personal appeal. The writer says he has written briefly, which is a literary understatement for so dense a letter. The mention of Timothy, the greeting from those from Italy and the final grace are the ordinary shape of an ancient letter's ending, and they are the clearest sign that this sermon was sent as a letter to a particular community.

The last words, "Grace be with all of you", match the way the letter began: the first word is God speaking, and the last is grace.
context.historical:
The letter's anonymity makes its closing the best source for the human setting. The writer asks the readers to pray for him, speaks of a clear conscience and a wish to live honourably, and hopes to be restored to them soon. This implies that he had been with them and was now, for some reason, kept apart, though the letter does not say why.

Timothy was a known companion of Paul and a familiar figure in the early church. The writer says that "our brother Timothy has been released", and the Greek verb can describe release from imprisonment or from some other kind of constraint, so we cannot be certain what happened. The note implies that the writer and the readers both knew Timothy, which places the letter in the circle of the apostles' associates, but it proves no authorship, since many people moved in that circle.

"Those from Italy send you greetings" can be read in two ways. It may mean that the writer was in Italy and the believers there send greetings, or that Italians living elsewhere send greetings to their home church. The phrase does not decide the matter, and the early tradition that the letter was connected with Rome rests on more than this verse.

The readers' leaders, mentioned again in verse 24, are greeted along with all the saints, which suggests an established community with recognised overseers. The setting is a church under pressure, which has already shown courage and whose leaders are watching over souls and giving an account, verse 17.
context.canonical:
The benediction draws deeply on the Old Testament. "The God of peace" is a phrase Paul uses repeatedly, Romans 15:33 and 1 Thessalonians 5:23 among them, and it points to the idea of shalom, wholeness. The eternal covenant has roots in the promises of an everlasting covenant, such as Isaiah 55:3, which speaks of an everlasting covenant with David, Jeremiah 32:40, where God promises never to turn away from doing good to His people, and Ezekiel 37:26, which speaks of a covenant of peace.

The shepherd imagery is among the most familiar in Scripture. God shepherds His flock in Psalm 23 and Isaiah 40:11. Ezekiel 34:23-25 has the LORD appoint one shepherd, His servant David, and make a covenant of peace with the flock, and Ezekiel 37:24-26 repeats the combination of one shepherd and a covenant of peace. The three elements of the benediction, peace, shepherd and eternal covenant, are all found together in these chapters. Isaiah 63:11 remembers God leading His people through the sea with the shepherds of His flock, and many readers have heard in Hebrews 13:20 an echo of that verse.

In the New Testament, Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and Peter calls Him the Chief Shepherd, 1 Peter 5:4. Zechariah 13:7, "Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered", was applied to Jesus by the Gospels. The equipping language links to Paul's words that God works in believers to will and to act, Philippians 2:13.

The phrase "blood of the covenant" itself goes back to Exodus 24:8 and forward to the words of Jesus at the Last Supper, Matthew 26:28.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer closes with a prayer because he knows that his own exhortation cannot do what it asks. He has told the readers to hold fast, to persevere, to come near and to go outside the camp, and now he turns and asks God to do in them what he has only been able to urge. This is a mark of a real preacher: the last word is not "try harder" but "may God equip you".

He also wants the readers to remember what the letter has said about Jesus, in a form they can carry. The long argument of thirteen chapters is compressed into a sentence they can pray: the God who raised Jesus, the great Shepherd, by the blood of the eternal covenant. It gives them a summary to take away.

The prayer carries a deliberate message about the source of Christian obedience. The writer asks God to equip them with everything good to do His will, and then he asks that God accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight. He puts himself in the "us". Obedience is something done by the readers and something done in them, and he does not separate the two.

The farewell shows that all of this is addressed to real people. The appeal to bear with the word of exhortation, the news of Timothy and the greetings are meant to remind the readers that the letter is the voice of a friend and a pastor, who wants to see them again.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The benediction is a prayer, not a command, and it should be read as such. It describes what God has done in raising Jesus and what He is able to do in His people, and it asks Him to do it. There is no instruction in it to be obeyed except the implied one: to pray the same prayer for each other.

The details of the farewell are descriptive and belong to the first readers. The mention of Timothy's release, the planned visit and the greetings from Italy tell us about the letter's setting, but they do not bind later readers. They are valuable because they show that the inspired letter was written in a human friendship.

The request in verse 22 that readers bear with the word of exhortation is the one explicit instruction, and it carries over. Believers in every age are asked to receive a hard word patiently. The letter has been demanding, and the final appeal reminds the reader that a long and searching sermon is a gift to be received, not an imposition to be avoided.

The point of the closing is also to correct a way of reading the commands of chapter 13 that would leave believers on their own. The equipping is God's work, so the obedience commanded is real but never self-powered.

debates.question: How does the resurrection relate to 'the blood of the eternal covenant'?

views.label: The blood is the basis on which Jesus was raised
views.case: The Greek says God brought Him back from the dead in, or by, the blood of the covenant. On this reading the Father's raising of Jesus is His public acceptance of the sacrifice, confirming that the covenant is in force and the sin offering has done its work. It fits chapters 9 and 10, where Jesus enters the true sanctuary by His own blood, 9:12.

views.label: The blood describes the covenant, not the raising
views.case: Others take the phrase as a description of the covenant that governs the whole sentence: the God who raised Jesus has done so as the shepherd of a flock bound to Him by the blood of an eternal covenant. The blood and the resurrection are then two linked parts of one saving story, not a technical claim about the means of the raising.

views.label: Both are held together
views.case: A third view holds that the Greek preposition is flexible enough to carry both ideas, so that the resurrection is the vindication of a sacrifice that has ratified the covenant. This is the view most commentaries take, with differences of emphasis.

debates.bearing: Whichever reading is preferred, the letter's logic is the same: the cross and the resurrection are not rivals. The blood establishes the covenant and the raising shows that God accepted it, so the Shepherd lives to lead His flock.

debates.question: Does the anonymity and the closing note affect how we read the letter's authority?

views.label: Authorship unknown, authority secure
views.case: The letter never names its author and the early church did not agree on one, but it was received as Scripture because of its content. Its authority rests on what it says, not on who wrote it, and ancient Christians were wary of assigning it to Paul with confidence.

views.label: A known apostolic circle
views.case: The reference to Timothy and to Italy places the writer within the apostolic circle, and some of the early church accepted the letter as apostolic on that ground. This supports the sense that the writer was well known to the readers.

views.label: Origen's view that only God knows
views.case: Origen of Alexandria is remembered for saying that who wrote the letter is known to God alone. It remains a sound answer for a reader who wants to avoid false confidence.

debates.bearing: The letter's claim on the reader does not depend on the name attached to it. Its argument, its use of Scripture and its Christ carry their own weight.

study.originalLanguages:
The benediction opens with ho theos tēs eirēnēs, "the God of peace". Eirēnē in the Greek Bible translates the Hebrew shalom, which means wholeness and well-being, not only the absence of conflict, so the writer is asking for a God who brings everything together. The title is Pauline in sound, as in Romans 15:33, but here it sits beside the language of resurrection and covenant.

The participle anagagōn, "brought back" or "brought up", describes the raising of Jesus. It is a word of lifting and leading, and that sits naturally beside the shepherd who follows in the same phrase. The letter's only direct statement of Jesus' resurrection is here, which is striking after so much said about His death, and it works as the crown of the argument.

Jesus is ton poimena ton megan, "the great shepherd". The adjective is the same one the letter uses of the great high priest, 4:14, and the writer joins the two offices together. The preposition en with haimati, "in the blood", is flexible; it can mean by means of, in the sphere of, or accompanied by, and this is the source of the debate about how the resurrection relates to the blood. The covenant is diathēkē aiōnios, "eternal", a word that stresses that it will not be replaced.

The verb katartisai, "equip", is a word with a practical background; in the Gospels it is used of mending nets, Mark 1:19, and it conveys making fit for use, putting in order and restoring. The prayer asks that the readers be made ready for the work of God's will. Its parallel verb poiōn, "doing" or "working", in verse 21 puts the action in God, who works in us what is euareston, "well pleasing", a word that was used in 13:16 of sacrifices and now returns, tying the readers' sacrifices to God's own work.

In verse 22 the writer says that he has written dia bracheōn, "in few words", and asks the readers to bear with, anechesthe, his logos paraklēseōs, "word of exhortation". The same phrase appears in Acts 13:15, where the BSB renders it "a word of encouragement", and the writer's own name for his work is a sermon. The last word, charis, "grace", is also the first and last theme of the letter.

typology.fulfillment: Israel's leaders were shepherds, and the LORD Himself was Israel's shepherd, as Psalm 23 and Isaiah 40:11 say. Ezekiel promised one shepherd, God's servant David, with a covenant of peace, Ezekiel 34:23-25 and 37:24-26. In Jesus the three strands meet: He is the Davidic king, the one in whom God Himself comes to shepherd, and the one who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. The escalation is that the shepherd dies and is raised, which no earlier shepherd could do. The type falls short in that Moses and David led the flock but could not bring it home; this Shepherd does, Revelation 7:17.

The covenants of the Old Testament, with Noah, Abraham, Israel and David, were all given by God and sealed in various ways, and the prophets spoke of a coming everlasting covenant, Isaiah 55:3 and Jeremiah 32:40. The covenant at Sinai was ratified with blood, Exodus 24:8. In Jesus the blood is His own and the covenant is eternal, because its mediator lives forever, 7:25. The correspondence is complete in form; the escalation is that this covenant does not need renewing and writes the law on hearts, as Jeremiah 31:33 promised. The old covenants fall short in being temporary, though they were genuine gifts.

typology.type: The God of peace who restores
typology.fulfillment: Shalom in the Old Testament includes the peace of a whole and secure community, and the prophets joined it to the covenant, Isaiah 54:10 and Ezekiel 37:26. In Hebrews the God of peace acts by raising Jesus, so peace is not only a mood but a rescue. In Christ the wholeness is offered to believers now and completed at the resurrection. The type is partial in that Israel's peace was often broken, and the peace the readers have is still being completed, as the prayer 'equip you' implies.

study.christ:
The benediction offers the fullest brief portrait of Christ in the letter. It names Him with His full title, our Lord Jesus, and speaks of Him in three ways: as the one raised from the dead, as the great Shepherd of the sheep, and as the mediator through whom God works and to whom glory belongs.

The resurrection is the new element. Hebrews has said much about His death and His entry into the heavenly sanctuary, and it has said that He lives forever to intercede, 7:25. Only here does it say directly that God brought Him back from the dead. The placing is deliberate. The letter's picture of Christ's finished work includes His rising as the Father's answer to His sacrifice. The covenant is eternal because its mediator cannot be held by death.

He is a Shepherd. In the Old Testament the shepherd was the title of kings and of God Himself, and Ezekiel promised a Davidic shepherd who would bring a covenant of peace. By calling Jesus the great Shepherd the writer says that He is that promised king, and that His flock is the people who hear His voice, John 10:11. He is great because He is greater than Moses, the shepherd of the sheep in the exodus, and greater than the earlier shepherds of Israel who failed. The writer has used this kind of comparison from the first chapters, in which Jesus is greater than angels, Moses, Aaron and the covenant itself.

The Shepherd who dies and is raised is also the one who wraps the community in His care. John says that He lays down His life for the sheep, and the Revelation says that the Lamb in the centre of the throne will be their shepherd, Revelation 7:17. The two pictures, Lamb and Shepherd, belong together here: the one who was slain is the one who leads.

Finally, the whole prayer is "through Jesus Christ". God equips and accomplishes through Him, and the glory goes to Him. The letter ends where it began, with the Son as the one through whom God acts.

A caution: not every verse of the benediction hides a code. The links are those the passage itself provides, the shepherd, the blood, the covenant and the raising.
study.god:
The God of the final blessing is the God of peace. The title tells us that He is not a God of conflict or of mere power but of well-being. The peace is not a feeling of calm but the shape of His work: He brings what was broken back into wholeness. He does this at the cost of a covenant sealed by blood, so His peace is neither cheap nor accidental.

He is the God who raises the dead. The verb is in the past, and the writer treats the raising of Jesus as a settled fact on which the community stands. God's power is not abstract; it has an event behind it. And since that event is the vindication of the Shepherd, the God who raises is also a God who keeps His covenant, which He declared eternal.

He is a God who equips. The prayer asks that He supply the readers with everything good to do His will. This reveals a God who does not command and then stand back. He gives what He asks. The Greek word for equipping carries the sense of putting things in order, mending, and furnishing, so it speaks of a God who attends to detail and restores what is damaged.

He works in us what pleases Him. It is one of the most striking doctrinal statements of the letter, and it is made in a prayer, not a lecture. Human obedience is real, and yet it is also His work, so that nothing is left for boasting. Paul says the same in Philippians 2:13, and the combination shows the shape of the Bible's teaching: we are called to obey and are enabled by the one who commands.

He is worthy of eternal glory. The doxology is addressed to Jesus Christ, and it closes a letter that began by saying that the Son is the radiance of God's glory. For worship the passage teaches that the proper end of theology is praise. The letter finishes with Amen, and the reader is expected to join it, trusting that the God of peace who has begun to work will complete what pleases Him.

crossReferences.note: The people remember Moses and ask where the One is who brought them through the sea with the shepherds of His flock. Many readers hear an echo of this verse in Hebrews 13:20, where God brings back the great Shepherd, so that Jesus is the greater Moses and the greater exodus.

The LORD promises one shepherd, His servant David, and a covenant of peace. It contains the same three elements as the benediction, shepherd, covenant and peace, and helps explain why the writer joins them in one sentence.

David will be king and one shepherd for all, and God will make a covenant of peace that is everlasting. It is the fullest Old Testament form of the picture in Hebrews 13:20, with the promise of permanence that the word eternal carries.

God invites the thirsty to come and promises an everlasting covenant, the loving devotion promised to David. It shows that the idea of an eternal covenant was already tied to David's line, which Hebrews finds fulfilled in Jesus.

God promises an everlasting covenant in which He will never turn away from doing good and will put His fear in their hearts. It explains how the covenant can be eternal: God Himself secures the people's faithfulness, which is what the benediction asks for.
Moses sprinkles blood on the people and says, 'This is the blood of the covenant.' The covenant at Sinai was ratified with blood, and Hebrews points to a better blood that ratifies a better covenant.

Jesus says He is the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. It is the clearest New Testament statement that the shepherd's death is part of his care, and it fits the Shepherd of Hebrews who is raised by the blood of the covenant.

Peter speaks of the Chief Shepherd who will appear and give the crown of glory. It shows that the title shepherd was used of Jesus in the early church, and it points to His return in the way Hebrews points to His raising.

God works in you to will and to act for His good purpose. It parallels the prayer that God would accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight, and it supports the reading that obedience is both commanded and given.
Paul prays that the God of peace Himself will sanctify the readers completely and keep them blameless. It is the same kind of prayer, asking God to do what the letter urges, with the same title.

The LORD calls for the sword to strike the Shepherd so that the sheep are scattered. Jesus applied this to the night of His arrest, and Hebrews shows the other side: the struck Shepherd is brought back from the dead.

The Lamb in the centre of the throne will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water. It carries the picture of the great Shepherd to its end, when He gathers His people into the presence of God.

study.oneStory:
The closing sentence of Hebrews places the whole story of Scripture into a single prayer. It starts with God, the God of peace, who is the source of everything in creation and who intended His world to be a place of wholeness. Sin broke that peace in Genesis 3, and the history that follows is the history of broken relationships with God and with one another. The prayer names God as the one who has acted to restore it.

The covenants of the Old Testament are in the background. God made promises to Noah, Abraham, Israel and David, and each promised more than the last. The prophets looked to a day when God would make a covenant of peace with a shepherd king, Ezekiel 34:25, and an everlasting covenant that He would keep in His people, Jeremiah 32:40. The prayer says that this is what has now been done. The eternal covenant is sealed by the blood of Jesus and attested by His resurrection.

The shepherd theme runs from Genesis, where Abel keeps flocks and Jacob speaks of God as the one who shepherded him, through Moses and David, to the prophets' hope. It arrives in Jesus, who is the shepherd who dies and lives, and it continues to the end, when the Lamb will be the shepherd of the redeemed, Revelation 7:17.

The prayer also looks forward. To equip the readers and to work in them what pleases God is the present stage of a work that will be completed at the resurrection, when peace is made whole. The God of peace is the one who finishes what He begins, Philippians 1:6. And the letter's closing words, glory forever and ever, are the same words that the whole new creation will sing. The story ends not with the readers' efforts but with God's, and in a doxology that has no end.

quiz.q: How does the benediction describe what God did for Jesus?

options.text: The God of peace brought Him back from the dead as the great Shepherd, by the blood of the eternal covenant.
options.note: Verse 20 names the resurrection of the great Shepherd.

options.text: God raised Him from the dead by His mighty power.
options.note: True and central, and the benediction adds that He did so through the blood of the eternal covenant, as the great Shepherd.

options.text: God made Him an ordinary shepherd.
options.note: He is the great Shepherd of the sheep, not merely ordinary.
The resurrection is by the blood of the eternal covenant, not its abandonment.

quiz.q: What does the writer pray God will do for the readers?

options.text: Equip them with every good thing to do His will and work in them what pleases Him.
options.note: Verse 21 is the heart of the prayer.

options.text: Work in them what is pleasing in His sight.
options.note: This is genuinely part of the prayer, which also asks God to equip them with every good thing to do His will.
The prayer is for equipping to do God's will, not for comfort.
It goes beyond forgiveness to God equipping and working in them.

quiz.q: What title for Jesus does the benediction use, and what does it convey?

options.text: The great Shepherd of the sheep, who leads and keeps His flock.
options.note: Verse 20 calls Him the great Shepherd, raised to tend His people.

options.text: The Shepherd raised from the dead for His flock.
options.note: True, He is the risen Shepherd, and the specific title used is the great Shepherd of the sheep, supreme over the flock.
He is the great Shepherd, supreme over the flock.

options.text: A distant owner uninvolved with the sheep.
options.note: He is the Shepherd who tends and keeps His sheep.

quiz.q: How does the writer describe his own letter in verse 22?

options.text: A word of exhortation, written briefly, which he urges them to bear with.
options.note: Verse 22 calls the letter a word of exhortation.

options.text: A serious message he hopes they will take to heart.
options.note: True in tone, and specifically he calls it a word of exhortation, written only briefly, that he urges them to bear with.

options.text: A private message for one person.
options.note: It is addressed to the whole community.

options.text: An exhaustive treatise leaving nothing out.
options.note: He says he has written only briefly, not exhaustively.

questions: God equips you with everything good to do His will. Where do you need to trust Him to supply what obedience requires rather than relying on your own strength?
Jesus is the great Shepherd raised from the dead. How does knowing your Shepherd is alive and leading you shape your week?
God works in His people what is pleasing in His sight. How does it free you to know your obedience is finally His gift and work?
The letter is a word of exhortation to be heeded. Having studied Hebrews, what one truth most calls for a change in how you live?
The letter ends with grace. How does resting in God's grace, rather than your performance, send you out to serve Him with joy?

translationNotes.note: 'Brought back from the dead' is the one explicit mention of the resurrection in the letter; it crowns the earlier emphasis on Christ's finished sacrifice and enthronement.
'Equip' translates katartizō, used of mending nets or setting a bone; it pictures God putting His people fully in order to do His will.

'Those from Italy send you greetings' is ambiguous, and may mean either the writer is in Italy or that Italian believers away from home send greetings back; it does not settle the letter's origin, and the author remains unnamed.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Hebrews 13:20-25. The authorship of Hebrews is unknown and is not asserted as Pauline. Sermon set to none; no expositor series confirmed this session.
